title: Bottleshaped Cistern: 18th-Century Rainwater Storage in an Old House (This Old House)
summary: This Old House features historic archaeologist Suzanne Shere examining an intact, bottleshaped cistern serving as a rainwater storage system for an 18th-century house. The segment describes how the cistern was built with handmade brick, likely two bricks thick, and how bricks appear to have been reused from a chimney or fireplace. It notes the absence of a builder’s trench, mortared joints to the bottom, and a waterproof bottom surface capped with a thin paving-like layer. A large top opening suggests a trap-door for manual bucket access or a crank draw, and interior inspection reveals a depth of about seven feet and a lead pipe connected to the house basement for water delivery to a spigot. The discussion places the cistern within a broader domestic water ecosystem of the period, including wells, privies, and gardens, illustrating how early households managed water for washing, drinking, and chores within spatial constraints.
topics: reused bricks from chimney or fireplace
archaeological interpretation of domestic water systems

sections.title: Discovery and Identification
sections.description: The archaeologist identifies the feature as a cistern intended to collect and store water for household tasks, distinct from a well.

sections.title: Brickwork and Foundation Details
sections.description: Observations describe brick thickness, signs of reuse, absence of a builder's trench, and mortaring that secures the bottom against natural subsurface soil.

sections.title: Top Access and Opening
sections.description: The feature has a large top opening likely fitted with a cover, enabling bucket access or a crank-style draw for retrieving water.

sections.title: Interior Form and Waterproofing
sections.description: Interior inspection confirms the bottleshape and notes a ~7-foot depth, with a bottom waterproofing layer and visible lead pipe, suggesting a watertight interior and a connection to the house.
